introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Answer FOUR questions in all. Answer question ONE and three others, choosing at least ONE question from SECTION B and TWO from SECTION C. Question ONE carries thirty-one marks and the rest carry twenty-three marks each.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Candidates are advised NOT to attempt the questions on field investigations if such an exercise has not been carried out.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Calculators are allowed.

Materials required: Topographic map, graph paper and two outline maps of Cameroon.

questions.enonce_markdown: 5. a) Show how the two main seasons of Cameroon's climate are the result of the influence of air masses from different sources. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Air masses and the ITCZ.** Cameroon lies in the tropics, and its seasons are controlled by two air masses that meet along the **Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)**; the ITCZ follows the overhead sun, moving north from about March to July and south from about September to January.

**1. The wet (rainy) season - tropical maritime air.**

- *Source*: the south Atlantic Ocean (the St Helena high pressure), which gives the **south-west monsoon** winds.
- *Characteristics*: warm, very humid and unstable air, which blows landward from the Gulf of Guinea, rises over the coast and the highlands, cools and condenses, giving heavy rain (relief rainfall as well as convectional rain).
- *Timing*: when the ITCZ lies north of the country (about April to October in the south and May to September in the north) this air mass covers Cameroon. Rainfall is highest in the south-west (Mount Cameroon area) and decreases northwards because the air loses moisture and the season is shorter.

**2. The dry season - tropical continental air.**

- *Source*: the Sahara Desert (the Azores / Saharan high pressure), which gives the dry **north-east trade winds (the Harmattan)**.
- *Characteristics*: hot by day, dry, dusty and stable air that brings no rain, low humidity and hazy skies.
- *Timing*: when the ITCZ moves south (about November to March), this air mass covers the north, and in the south during the same period dry conditions prevail with some haze; the dry season is long in the north (about 6 months or more) and short in the south.

**Result.** The two seasons alternate because the ITCZ and the two air masses shift north and south; the south, where the ITCZ passes twice, has two rainy seasons separated by a short dry season, and the north has one rainy and one long dry season.

*Marks: air mass 1 source and characteristics 2 + 2; ITCZ movement 1; timing/areas affected 1.*

questions.enonce_markdown: b) Examine the distribution of manufacturing industries in the Northern Lowlands of Cameroon. (8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**General pattern.** Manufacturing in the northern lowlands (the Benue basin and the Chad basin, the North and Far North Regions) is small in scale and **clustered in a few towns**, mostly agro-industries processing local raw materials; it is much less developed than in the Littoral and Centre.

**Main concentrations and types (5 marks).**

- **Garoua and Maroua (the regional centres)**: cotton ginning and textile and clothing manufacture (CICAM at Garoua), cotton-seed oil mills and soap, breweries and soft drinks, abattoirs, leather and tanning, the printing and construction industries.
- **Cotton-growing towns (for example Guider, Kaele, Touboro and other places)**: ginneries of the cotton company (SODECOTON), sited in the heart of the cotton fields.
- **Rice-growing plains (Yagoua and the Logone-Chari area)**: rice mills attached to the irrigated rice schemes.
- **Figuil**: the cement plant, located next to the limestone deposits.
- **Elsewhere**: scattered small enterprises (grain mills, bakeries, carpentry, brick-making, food and craft workshops), little heavy industry.

**Reasons (3 marks).** Raw materials (cotton, rice, livestock, limestone), the large cattle and cotton output, and the Lagdo dam power on the Benue; the markets in the towns and in neighbouring Chad and Nigeria; labour; the transport axes (the roads from Ngaoundere); and the colonial and state planning of cotton schemes. Constraints: remoteness from the ports, poor roads, shortage of capital and of electricity, and recent insecurity in the Far North.

*Marks: pattern 2; named examples and types 3; reasons 3.*

questions.enonce_markdown: c) Discuss TWO problems associated with the exploitation of water resources in Cameroon and suggest TWO measures to cope with the problems identified. (9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Problem 1: water pollution (and the resulting scarcity of safe water).**

- Industrial effluents, domestic sewage and refuse, agricultural chemicals and oil spills pollute rivers, lakes and wells, especially in the large cities (Douala, Yaounde) and around plantations and mines.
- *Consequences*: water-borne diseases (cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea), destruction of fish and plants, high cost of treatment, and shortage of safe water for the population.

**Problem 2: uneven distribution, seasonal shortage and inadequate infrastructure.**

- The south has water all the year round, while the north has a long dry season, falling rivers and a shrinking Lake Chad; many rural and peri-urban areas have no taps or boreholes, so women and children walk long distances for water.
- The dams and water systems (Lagdo, Song Loulou, Edea) are costly; the water supply network of the towns is old and poorly maintained and cannot follow the rapid urban growth, and the poor have little access.
- Other related problems: flooding downstream of dams, siltation caused by deforestation and farming, conflicts between farmers, herders and fishermen (Lake Chad), and the use of water for hydroelectricity versus irrigation.

**Measures (about 3 marks each).**

1. *To cope with pollution*: apply the law (water code, the polluter-pays principle), build waste-water and sewage treatment plants, control industrial effluents, collect refuse, educate the public, and protect the water sources and catchments (reafforestation and buffer zones along rivers).
2. *To cope with shortage and uneven supply*: drill boreholes and wells in the dry areas, build small dams and reservoirs, collect rainwater, extend and repair the urban water network (public-private partnerships, community water committees), use irrigation methods that save water, and co-operate with neighbouring states through the Lake Chad Basin Commission.

*Marks: two problems discussed 2 x 3 = 6 (explanation and example); two measures 2 x 1.5 = 3.*
